topics.title: Completed actions
topics.description: 了 for what just happened, 过 for what you've ever done

guide.intro: A1 introduced 了 briefly. A2 is where it really earns its keep. There are also two siblings to learn — 过 (experience) and 还没 (not yet) — that round out talking about the past.

sections.text: 了 — completed action
Tack 了 onto a verb to mark that the action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to a past tense, but technically it's an aspect marker — the action is complete, not necessarily long ago.

rows.source: 我 吃 饭。
我 吃 了 饭。
他 来 了。

sections.text: Negation: 还没 (not yet)
Don't pair 了 with 不/没. To say "haven't done it", drop 了 and use 还没 (hái méi):

rows.source: 我 还没 吃。
他 还没 来。

sections.text: 过 — experience marker
过 (guò) tags a verb as "have you ever done this in your life?" — it's about experience, not completion. Compare:

rows.source: 我 吃 过 北京 烤鸭。
我 吃 了 北京 烤鸭。

sections.text: Rule of thumb: 了 = the action is wrapped up. 过 = at some point in your life this happened. They occasionally co-occur but you'll mostly pick one.

topics.title: Shopping
topics.description: Money, prices, and getting what you want

guide.intro: Real Chinese shopping is fast and friendly. Three phrases get you 80% of the way there: 多少钱 (how much), 太贵了 (too expensive), and 给我 (give me).

sections.text: Money words
Spoken Chinese uses 块 (kuài) for the main currency unit; written and formal Chinese uses 元 (yuán). They're the same value — like "buck" vs "dollar". 毛 (máo) and 分 (fēn) are tenths and hundredths.
Asking the price

rows.source: 多少 钱？
这个 多少 钱？
十块。
太贵了！

exercises.prompt: Which is the casual word for "yuan"?

lessons.title: Buy & sell
lessons.description: 买 and 卖 — easy to mix up

exercises.explanation: 买 (mǎi, 3rd tone) = buy. 卖 (mài, 4th tone) = sell. Tone is the only difference!

exercises.prompt: Build "I want to buy a book"
exercises.answer: 我 要 买 一 本 书
exercises.explanation: 本 (běn) is the measure word for books.

exercises.prompt: Shop owner says "五块" — what is the price?

exercises.answer: 给 我 两 个
exercises.explanation: Use 两 (liǎng, "a pair of") rather than 二 (èr) before measure words like 个.

topics.title: Comparisons
topics.description: A is bigger than B — the 比 pattern

guide.intro: English uses "-er" or "more" for comparisons. Mandarin uses 比 (bǐ) — a single particle that does the same job, with a fixed word order: A 比 B + adjective.

sections.text: Basic pattern: A 比 B + adjective

rows.source: 我 比 他 高。
苹果 比 香蕉 便宜。
今天 比 昨天 热。

sections.text: Don't add 很 / 不 / 是 to a 比 sentence. "我 比 他 很 高" is wrong — drop 很. The comparison itself does the work.
Even more: 更
Add 更 (gèng, "even more") before the adjective when comparing to an already-strong baseline:

rows.source: 他 比 我 更 高。
rows.translation: He is even taller than me.

sections.text: The most: 最
最 (zuì) before an adjective means "the most". No 比 needed — it's a superlative.

rows.source: 他 最 高。
我 最 喜欢 茶。

sections.text: Negative: A 没有 B + adjective
To say "A is NOT as ___ as B", flip to 没有 (méi yǒu, "doesn't have"):

rows.source: 我 没有 他 高。
rows.translation: I am not as tall as him.

exercises.explanation: 对不起 (sorry) softens the refusal. 没时间 = don't have time.
下次吧 — literally "next time, eh?" Common gentle decline.
改天 — literally "change day". The Chinese version of "rain check".

topics.title: Connecting ideas
topics.description: And, but, because, so — stitch sentences together

guide.intro: Up to now most sentences have been one thought. A2 is where you start chaining: "I went and then I ate", "It rained but I went", "I'm tired because I worked". Mandarin makes this easy — a small set of connectors does most of the heavy lifting.

sections.text: 然后 — and then
然后 (rán hòu) chains two events in time. Use it to narrate sequences.

rows.source: 我 起床，然后 吃 早饭。
rows.translation: I get up, and then I eat breakfast.

sections.text: 但是 / 可是 — but
Both mean "but" with no real difference; 可是 is a touch more conversational.

rows.source: 我 想 去，但是 我 没 时间。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dànshì wǒ méi shíjiān.
rows.translation: I want to go, but I don't have time.

sections.text: 因为...所以 — because...so
Mandarin often uses both halves where English uses just one ("I'm tired BECAUSE I worked" → 因为 我 工作 了，所以 我 很 累).

rows.source: 因为 下雨，所以 我 没 去。
rows.pinyin: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ méi qù.
rows.translation: Because it was raining, (so) I didn't go.

sections.text: You can drop one half if context is clear: "因为 下雨，我 没 去" works too. The full pair just sounds slightly more emphatic.
或者 vs 还是 — both mean "or"
Easy mix-up. 或者 (huò zhě) goes in statements ("I want tea or coffee"). 还是 (hái shi) goes in questions ("Do you want tea or coffee?").

rows.source: 我 想 喝 茶 或者 咖啡。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē chá huòzhě kāfēi.
rows.translation: I want to drink tea or coffee. (statement)

rows.source: 你 想 喝 茶 还是 咖啡？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng hē chá háishi kāfēi?
rows.translation: Do you want tea or coffee? (choice question)
